utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Now we are sitting in Courtroom I. That might be a test, if this courtroom is perhaps more convenient because, in the near future, there are not so many trials in this Tribunal, and we can see how it works. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has additional questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yesterday, you gave us information about who was involved in the evacuation operation of Zepa. My follow-up question to that is: Who was the overall in charge of this operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends who -- as far as the UN was concerned, I was in charge of the operation. But that was only the UN element. There was still -- I didn't control the people, I didn't control the BiH, the Bosnian army, or any elements of theirs, or the Bosnian Serbs. And we were all involved in the -- in the affair. But for the actual sort of command of the UN forces, then that would have been me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. In your view, then, was the evacuation successful? Did it go well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Given that it had to happen, we were able to remove the vast -- and certainly all the women and children from harm's way in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next question relates to Srebrenica, actually, and in the Prosecution's summary, you -- according to the Prosecution summary, you had been on leave but was recalled on 11th July and arrived at UNPROFOR headquarters in the early hours of 12th July. And then it goes on to quote you as saying, by the end of 13th July, you believed that the BiH had broken out of the enclave. From what I have read, am I right in thinking that there were active combat actions or activities going on in the enclave prior to that the between the BiH and the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. The BiH -- the Bosnian army, had attacked out of Srebrenica. I was saying it was in early June. It turned out it was -- I beg your pardon, in early July. It was in late June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: So when you say that the -- the BiH had broken out of the enclave, where did they go? Do you have information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, my understanding was that they had broken out in the general direction of Tuzla. The -- I am clearer now, as a result of other reporting and so forth, that that was very broadly the -- the direction. But there was a much more -- people went in a number of directions. Some went to Zepa. And the -- but my understanding at that particular period that they had broken out in a north-easterly direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think this is the last one, and more a general question. In the war situation where there are a lot of casualties, but with particular reference to the wars in the former Yugoslavia starting from 1991, what happens to the war dead, the people who get killed in a war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are we referring to the combatants or the civil population amongst whom they are fighting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I'm particularly interested in the combatants.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a general rule, this is an -- and most armies appear to have this, certainly those I have served in or alongside, there is a process of recovering your dead and burying them and accounting for where they're buried because subsequently they're often dug up and the bodies are centralised or got home to their -- to their dependants. So that's the sort of general procedure, but the precise details will differ with the army and the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Do you know what happened in the particular case of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was -- again, where I could observe this, was with the Bosnian army, and particularly in the vicinity of Sarajevo, then bodies were buried and usually by their dependants because the soldier came from that particular vicinity. But not always. And there was also -- a process which I was aware of, but this was conducted by the civil affairs people of the UN, a process by which bodies were exchanged. The exchange between the two sides, usually for a fee, as to -- and so that they could be buried by their dependants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you, General Smith, for your clarifications. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't receive interpretation at the moment. Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General Smith. I do have a question for you relating to what you said yesterday which is recorded on page 52 of the transcript, according to the page numbering of the transcript yesterday. According to the officer in charge of civil affairs, Mr. David Harland, it was to be expected that most of the people going out of Zepa should be captured. However, you had said that this was not the case and that there was a possibility for these people to get out with no harm. So this -- the contradiction in these statements surprises me slightly, especially coming from someone so extremely credible among the people who were on the ground. Therefore, I would like to ask you, based on your experience on the ground, the following question: You had contacts with people from the ABiH and with General Mladic and his assistants, and, of course, also with Muslim representatives. So was there any will to exterminate or kill or capture Muslim soldiers, once they had been separated from women, children, and elderly people, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I should go back to the -- the beginning of your question to try and sort out this, if you like, apparent confusion between David Harland and I, and I thought I had touched on it in another of my answers. The first point to make is that David Harland is the civil affairs officer of Sector Sarajevo. Sector Sarajevo had responsibility for the Zepa enclave on a day-to-day basis. The Ukrainian's forces were under command of Sector Sarajevo. Sector Sarajevo provided the French forces that I had in Zepa with me. But I -- I was aware, and David Harland was not aware, that Carl Bildt in Belgrade had been conducting a negotiation so -- so that the people who had -- were hiding up in the high ground in the mountains in Zepa could exfiltrate out over the river Drina and in Serbia and thus to a form of safety. They would still be interned, they would still be detained, but it would be possible for the ICRC to register them and monitor the -- what happened to them. David Harland did not know that that negotiation was going on, but I did. So our point of view about the safety of the people of military age, whether they were armed or not, was different, because our knowledge was different. The second point is that, if -- it isn't a question of whether or not they had not been captured or not, I just saw that there was a possibility of them being able to exfiltrate out of the enclave and into Serbia. I was quite clear that if they started to try and move in any other direction, then there was a high probability that they would be captured or killed. Whether or not they could have been or would have been killed or captured, I cannot say. But my supposition, particularly as we were beginning to get increasingly clear that the missing men from Srebrenica were not alive, was that they would be killed if they were taken. Either killed in the taking or killed on being taken. And, hence, Carl Bildt's negotiations with Serb -- Serbia, in order to try and get them to be able to exfiltrate over the Drina. Does that explain my understanding of the position at the time, but also the difference between David Harland's reporting, which is the reporting of the subordinate headquarters, to my understanding of the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. This is a sufficient answer for me for the time being. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, now you may commence your cross-examination. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Peace on to this house and may this day in court and the final judgement reflect God's will. I would like to greet Mr. Smith and wish him a pleasant stay here in our midst and I would like to congratulate him on his retirement and wish him a life of peace and happiness among his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to start with the questions that were put to you by Judge Mindua and Judge Nyambe. First of all, I believe it would be fair, both from your side and mine, if we were to tell the truth about the role of Slobodan Milosevic in these events. Because, in these proceedings, as we see on the basis of different notes, and on the basis of the statements of many witnesses who are protected, a reference was made to the role of Serbia and Slobodan Milosevic using the vocabulary that was used in wartime you and I know. I would like you to ask you to tell this Trial Chamber clearly whether Serbia made it possible for all of those who wanted to cross the Drina to go into Serbia and then to move on to third countries in accordance with their wishes. Do you know about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, those that crossed the Drina were interned and then subsequently moved to other countries or, at the end of the war, back to their homes. Or back into Bosnia. I am not sure what the proportions are. And my knowledge of this is -- is anecdotal rather than having read it or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether Mr. Slobodan Milosevic and Serbia were the ones who actually resolved this problem for these people who wanted to get out but not surrender to the Army of Republika Srpska? And did he keep confidential all this information before this actually happened? And did the international community mediate in resolving this humanitarian issue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know details of the negotiation or who Mr. Bildt was actually talking to, and I think the information was kept confidential but, again, I don't know that. It -- it certainly wasn't discussed, as it were, in my presence in Bosnia during the rest of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for having said this. Just tell me another thing. Could somebody negotiate in Serbia, could anybody negotiate in Serbia, except for Slobodan Milosevic about the arrival of some other troops into his country and with or without involving international organisations like the Red Cross and the army and the police, et cetera? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you asked me whether -- who the negotiation was taking place with. I don't know who that was. I'm -- I am quite prepared to believe that the process of this negotiation was reported up to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us now, tell the Trial Chamber, when you found out that such negotiations were under way? I'm referring to the actual date when you found out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but I think it was after the London Conference. So it would be sometime after the weekend of the 23rd of July, which I think was a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In order for us not to look at Harland's reports, as was the case yesterday, and in order for us not to read them and not to see what corresponds to what - he after all made the assessments that he made - I would like to ask you -- or, rather, you said that you saw General Mladic carrying in his hands the agreement, on the basis of which the Muslims accepted the evacuation of civilians. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there was such an agreement. I can't remember when I said that I saw him carrying it in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us when this agreement came into existence, when the Muslims signed it, and when he agreed to allow all the Muslims to leave Zepa, as you had said? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I -- I -- I don't recall the dates of these events that clearly, but I think this occurred after the -- the London Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since I think -- or, rather, was this before the 23rd, before the negotiations started in Serbia regarding the evacuation of civilians and soldiers from Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a recollection of the precise chronology of this -- these events to be able to tell you whether I learnt of the negotiation before I saw any written agreement or signed agreement between Mladic and the population in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us when you found out from the Muslims that they wished to leave Zepa safely? Which is why the negotiations did take place in Belgrade. I mean Bildt negotiating. When did you find that out from the Muslims in Sarajevo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I'm pausing because I have a -- I don't think -- I don't agree with you that the negotiations in Belgrade was a direct result of people wanting to leave Zepa. The reason, I understood, Mr. Bildt started his negotiations was because we had the group of men up in the mountains separated from the women and children. Again, we'd have to -- I'd have to look at some diary or record of reporting, but I think I understood that the women and children wished to be evacuated from Zepa fairly early, probably immediately after my return from the London Conference. But it might have been just before. But my -- my belief is that it was immediately after the London Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand you. Nobody can remember exact dates but what is important for us is this: You remember that Carl Bildt knew that the Muslim soldiers who had been separated from the women wanted to cross to the other territory and that was the gist of his negotiations with Slobodan Milosevic, which ended up in a positive way, and everybody still alive. So could you tell us: When was it approximately that he received information from the Muslim side that those soldiers wanted to go and cross into Serbia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he received from the Muslim side. He was certainly seeing my headquarters, the reporting from my headquarters. I don't know what he -- if he was talking to the Muslim side or he received anything from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you know whether those soldiers were informed that they could go to Serbia and that they would not be facing arms over there, but, rather, they would be registered and processed properly. Was that known to them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- again, I don't know that it was known to them. I can suppose that since a number of them crossed the Drina this option -- they were aware of this option. How they came to be aware of it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you said that you knew that a door was open, and now I'm asking you: It means that those soldiers should have been informed one way or the other that a door was open for them to cross into Serbia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just because I know the door is open doesn't follow that I know how it was opened or whether anyone else knows it's open.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But it was sufficient that you knew, because you were a UN representative, one of the persons who took part in the whole negotiation -- negotiating process. So it is also probable that other people knew about it as well, people who took part in the effort to bring this to a successful resolution. So is there a possibility that somebody, after the London Conference, took the initiative in order to bring this to a successful fruition or is it, on the other hand, possible that everything happened spontaneously? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, I know that Carl Bildt was conducting this negotiation and I knew it at the time. I knew that it had achieved the -- the result that it was possible for people to cross the Drina. How this was done, who informed who other than the -- that I was told that this limited information that the negotiation was under way, I have no other knowledge at all, and I didn't have any at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, on page 51, I wouldn't know what the official numeration is, in line 6 you said: "I had evidence that people were crossing into Serbia." So while your other associates in good faith didn't know anything about it and wrote their reports, such as Harland did, you said that you had evidence about people crossing. So I would like you to tell the Trial Chamber a little bit more about this. What is it that you were trying to say when you said that? Because I think that the Trial Chamber has to have a fuller picture, and maybe it would be better for us to avoid going through all the documents and all the reports page by page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the setting of what you are quoting me as saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have yesterday's page 51 on the screen. From line 6 onwards, or maybe even from line 1 onwards. Then the witness will be able to see what exactly he said and then clarify. Lines 12 and 13. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you take a look at the whole page, 51, and then can you tell us exactly what was it you were trying to say there.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I -- we're talking about one of Harland's reports, and I'm trying to explain why this is -- again, why my view of the situation at the time and decisions I'm making aren't exactly the same view as that expressed by Harland. And my -- and I'm saying here at this point that I have those -- that information. Presumably I was told this. I can't remember who I was told it by, possibly Carl Bildt. And that's all I needed to know at that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I think just to orient everybody a little bit if we go back a couple pages. I don't think this will be a dispute. This is a report that's dated 2 August just so we can put some time-frame on the question that General Tolimir is putting to General Smith. It's Zepa report number 15 that General Smith was talking about, dated 2 August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm not sure if we can move the transcript of yesterday at the moment, because this was just deleted because of the re-numbering of the pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Registry is trying to keep the transcript of yesterday -- the Registry is trying to keep the transcript of yesterday with the numbering of the pages in the old-fashioned way so that it is easier for you to put questions to relevant parts of the transcript of yesterday. Now we have the new numbering but there is also the -- the other -- old version. Now we can see it again, page 51. Mr. Thayer made the proposal to go some pages back to see -- I think we can see it here. On page 50, lines 16 and the following. Tab -- he said yesterday: "Tab 17 in the English version." And then we can see line 22: "We can see from the date, it's 2nd of August 1995. Report from David Harland ..." Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Thayer. I really have to apologise. However, I don't speak the English language and I don't know exactly what is on the screen at any given moment. So can we look at page 52 [Realtime transcript read in error "352"] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is no reason for any apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. So can we show to the witness page 52 where, in line 6, he said: "I was not so much worried about what was going to happen because I knew that the back door was going to be open for them to cross to Serbia." So, based on this, my question is -- and the witness should answer only after he read the relevant part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I would like to make a correction in the transcript. It says "page 352," but we heard clearly the interpretation, "page 52." We should have the full page 52 on the screen, please, if possible. Thank you. Now put your question, please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is what I would like to know about: When exactly did this happen? What is the operative time? We had different reports at different times about the events in Zepa. So when exactly were you slightly less worried about what was going to happen because you knew that the back door was open to Serbia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the timings. All of these remarks, as it has already been pointed out, is me trying to explain the difference between the Harland report and my previous statements and the reporting from my headquarters. I don't remember at what point I am slightly less worried than David Harland. That's the point I'm trying to explain here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it during the negotiations about Zepa evacuation? Am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some point, it -- we have this negotiation going on which allows people -- eventually will allow people to cross the Drina. What I am trying to explain in this exchange that is in front of me and occurred yesterday is the difference of the reporting between David Harland and my understanding of what was going on, because I was privy to a piece of information that he did not have. And this meant that I was, in contrast to him, less concerned than he was about those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know at the time that the Muslims in the forests, separated from their families, and generally the Muslim representatives who were aware of the situation and the negotiations conducted by Mr. Bildt, did you know that they were going to be saved by crossing the Drina river? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know they would be saved. I knew that this option was, in the first instance, being negotiated, and then the negotiations had succeeded at some later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So this is not really that important to us and the Trial Chamber. But while the negotiations were going on, did you know that they were going on?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean that while my negotiations are going on, did I know that Carl Bildt was negotiating?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The exact time is not that important to me. What is important is that you said that the negotiations in Belgrade commenced after the London Conference, after the 23rd. So did you know after the 23rd that there were negotiations with the country of Serbia in order to achieve a safe passage of the Muslims from the Zepa enclave across the Drina river into Serbia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew, as I've said, that these negotiations were taking place. I think they started after the London Conference to give a -- the opportunity for people to exfiltrate out of Zepa over the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Muslim leadership in Sarajevo have certain information about the arrangements being made by Mr. Bildt and about the fact that the Muslim soldiers from Zepa would be saved and that the international community was taking part in those efforts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know and cannot speak for the information held by the Bosnian government in Sarajevo. It -- they must have known that at least the UN was taking part in these negotiations in Zepa because they knew I was involved in it, and I was telling them what I was doing. But other than that, I don't know what other information they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it discussed in the meeting on the 15th, when you were in Belgrade together with Mr. Bildt talking to the president of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, to Ratko Mladic and others? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was discussed? Zepa or the opening of a route over the Drina?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The opening of a route over the Drina. But also, if anything about Zepa was discussed and you know about it, could you tell us about it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall Zepa being discussed, except possibly as a place that needed the resupply by humanitarian convoys. I certainly don't remember any discussion about routes over the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So does that mean that this topic was discussed possibly only between Mr. Bildt and Mr. Milosevic, with the possibility of his closest associates also being present, in order to keep it all a secret? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there. Well, not there in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. A moment ago, when you were reminded about what you said yesterday on page 51 you said that you had evidence that people were crossing to Serbia. When did you receive the first evidence about it? And can you tell us when exactly you found out about it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am probably guilty of the misuse of the word "evidence." I -- my -- I don't remember being given evidence, like there was a list of people who had crossed or anything like that. What I think I remember being told was that some people had crossed. Crossed the Drina into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The word "evidence" is not that important for us. What is important is whether you had information about it. Thank you. So now we are going to see Exhibit 211. Excuse me -- thank you, Aleksandar. It's D111. And that's the list that you mentioned. So what I want to know is whether simply you had information about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a small correction on the transcript. In page 17, line 1, Mr. Tolimir said as reference to the transcript of yesterday, "it was on page 51," but this sentence was on page 52. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So bearing in mind all this, I want to know the following. So there was a flow of information that such a project was under way and that the UNPROFOR took part in it. Did you have any information on it? Were you aware of it? And is that the reason that you said that you were slightly less worried? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just explained that UNPROFOR was not part of -- of this project. I, as the commander UNPROFOR, was told that this negotiation was taking place. I did not involve the rest of my command in this process. I've told you what information I had on it and I was aware, but I cannot recall, and I am -- again say I was incorrect to use the word "evidence" in that -- that implies I had a concrete piece of paper or something. But I knew, or recall knowing, that some people had started to cross the Drina. I imagine, because I don't know, that I was told this by Mr. Bildt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution and not even me, nobody is going to take it against you the fact that you said, "I had evidence." That is simply a way of expression, you had information. We are not seeking evidence about it here. So here on our screen, in e-court, we see a document. This is a list of all persons who crossed into Serbia in accordance with that agreement. Can you also take a look at the second, the third, and the fourth page so that the witness could see for himself that not a single woman is on this list. Because yesterday you said that there were also some women who wanted to cross. So what I want to know is, did you have information about it? Or was it simply something that you were told by people who wanted to tell you that women were worried. I remember that Mr. Thayer even asked you whether there were some rapes, and you said that you didn't hear anything about it. So what I want us to see from this list is there were no women on this list and that not a single woman crossed into Serbia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In my view, we had not the right pages on the screen. In English it starts with number 31; in B/C/S, with number 38.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look at all the pages so that the witness can see for himself whether there are any women on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told that not all the pages have an English translation. But perhaps it is not necessary to see all names on the list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my limited memory of the names used in that part of the world, I have not seen a female name on the lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir, you have received your answer. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: If there are no women on this list, and, as you told us yesterday, you didn't hear that there were any rapes in Zepa, can we then agree that there were no women among those people and that they were all able-bodied men and they were not older than 60 at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree that of the list you've shown me, which purports to be a list of people who crossed the river Drina, there are no women amongst them. I didn't read the list to work out their ages, of the men. Nor does the list tell you whether they're all able-bodied or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we are not going to go into this. We are going to leave this task to the Trial Chamber and they're going to make their determination. My question for you is as follows. The BiH army also reported something that the Prosecution expert, Mr. Bezruchenko, mentioned in his report; namely, the fact that everybody left Zepa using various ways. Some of them went to Serbia; some of them went to the other side. So my question is as follows. Did you receive any information from the BiH army about the fate of the population and the soldiers of Zepa after the evacuation had been completed and after the UNPROFOR forces had left Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall receiving any information myself. It may have been received elsewhere in my command, but I don't recall any.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have the report by Mr. Bezruchenko, which is D55. Page 35, paragraph 123. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at line 6 of paragraph 123, which describes the situation of crossing over into Serbia. It reads as follows: "Led by Ramo Cardakovic and assistant for security, Salih Hasanovic, crossed into Serbia and surrendered to SRJ authorities. The number involved was 800 soldiers. The main body of the brigade split into several groups and each was acting to its own plan without centralised command. A group of about 200 men, under Hurim Sahic, succeeded to reach Kladanj across VRS-held territory on 2 August. Another group of about 50 men, originally from Visegrad, under Samir Cocalic set off for Gorazde or Priboj in Serbia. Another group of up to 300 soldiers originally from Srebrenica who arrived at Zepa after Srebrenica collapsed, went back to Srebrenica, hoping to break through to Tuzla along the same route used by the 28th Division. Yet another group about the size [sic] of a company under Sefik Zejnilovic went in the direction of Susice in the area of Crni Potok where it was going to stay for a long time. This plan was based on the fact that there was a big cache of food hidden in the area. A small group of about seven men crossed the VRS-held territory and joined the BiH army 243rd Motorised Brigade in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Corps. Another small group, numbering 14 soldiers reached Gorazde on 3 August." In footnote 183, Mr. Bezruchenko refers to the original document of the Army of B and H, speaking of the fact that everyone had left the enclave of Zepa. We can look at that report of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina which will tell us precisely who left and by what route. My question is this: Did you have any knowledge gained from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina about the fate of the inhabitants and soldiers of the enclave following their departure from the enclave and whether anyone remained behind?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have knowledge of the detail or specificity that you've just read out. The knowledge that I had was -- was that that was reported in the documents that emanated from my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina ever thank you for the mediation and protection offered by the UNPROFOR to their population in Zepa and for a successful rounding up of the entire operation?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall being thanked over this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter number 6039 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It is your letter of the 14th of July sent to General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I -- we have seen two documents today, D111, and D55. Astonishingly, they are not to be found on your list of exhibits to be used with this witness. I have received during this session the latest version, but I don't find it there. Please check it and all documents listed should be on the list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise for having omitted those. We will take note of your guidance. We will strive to remove any such problems.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Just for the accuracy of the record, 65 ter 6039 has been admitted into evidence yesterday as Prosecution Exhibit P2087. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the letter of protest of the 14th of July. In the first paragraph, you point out that there was an ultimatum issued for the evacuation of the Ukrainian soldiers from the enclave. Based on this letter of yours, can you recall who you received that information from, about the VRS requesting the UNPROFOR in Zepa to leave the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember how this information reached my headquarters, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I showed this document because the date is the 14th of July, and we will see in the next document, which is P596, and it is an internal memorandum of the UNPROFOR in Sarajevo, the date is the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2 in e-court, please. We're interested in paragraphs 8 through 11. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us when you've read it so that I can put my next question.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to read paragraph 8 downwards or the whole page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at paragraphs 8 through 11, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please let us know when the page should be turned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Please turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you managed to read that. Is this document, or the meeting referred to therein, the basis of your letter of protest sent to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know. It's going on in a different headquarters, but I imagine that they -- this -- the consequence of this meeting was then reported to my headquarters, and that's how I am taking action. But I can't recall the track of events at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you cannot recall it, I will not put any further questions about the topic. Do you perhaps recall whether General Mladic had sent a letter of protest to you, prior to your letter, whereby he addressed a situation in the enclave? If you cannot recall, it is 1D617, which can be used to jog your memory.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have that in e-court. Perhaps it will help the witness recall the letter sent to him by General Mladic on July 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is there a translation?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is no English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In that case, I will read it out so that it interpreted to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "I received your letter of July 9, 1995. The enclave of Srebrenica has not been demilitarised in keeping with the agreement of April 19 and May 8, 1993. The Muslims" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "The Muslims have not handed over their weapons, mines and explosives and combat assets to the UNPROFOR. The Muslim forces abused the special status accorded to their zone and the presence of your forces in order to prepare and carry out terrorist and other combat activities against the Serb population and territory of the RS."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "I wish to remind you that since that time and to date, the Muslim forces used attacks and infiltrated sabotage and terrorist groups in order to kill over 100 and wound some 200 Serb civilians. A number of Serb villages adjacent to the area were torched down with unthinkable massacres committed over civilians. In the last few days, they carried out a comprehensive military operation, in order to link up the enclaves in the area of the village of Zepa and burn down the villages of Visnjica and Banja Lucica. They killed the population. Even UNPROFOR members were not spared in the carrying out of their evil deeds. Although your forces were protecting them, they, too, became their victims." He concludes by saying: "I wish to convey to you that UNPROFOR members, as far as we are concerned will remain safe as they have been up to now. Signed by Ratko Mladic." Based on what I have read, I want to ask you this: Do you recall having received such letters in which General Mladic was addressing the situation with the Muslim armed forces and the activities they carried out or were carrying out from inside the enclave towards Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we referring to letters in general, or to Srebrenica and this particular set of circumstances in -- I'm not clear which the question is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I was asking you this: Did General Mladic send letters to you, trying to warn you of the enclaves Zepa and Srebrenica being used by Muslim soldiers to carry out attacks against Serb civilians.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall receiving some such letters. The -- when I received them, I am uncertain as to the timing of them, and I don't remember this particular letter that you have been reading to me. But, then, I was on leave on the date of this letter, so it is possible I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, I won't put any further such questions. I will remain with your yesterday's answer where you said that you and UNPROFOR representatives received a lot of information about attacks being carried out from the enclave out. Perhaps we can agree on that, and even the Prosecution do not dispute that the existence of the enclaves was abused, to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I apologise. I wanted to ask you whether the UNPROFOR had information about such attacks carried out from the Muslim enclaves into Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew that the Bosnian forces inside the enclaves were conducting attacks from those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were any UNPROFOR soldiers killed while you were in command by VRS soldiers to the extent of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: By VRS soldiers, yes, there was a -- there were people killed in Sarajevo on at least one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to the bridge at Vrbanja. For the time being, we'll stay with Zepa and Srebrenica. Could you please tell me that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica and Zepa, I don't recall an incident, no. And it wasn't Vrbanja bridge I was thinking of. It was a driver of a piece of engineer plant that I recall being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he killed on purpose, or was there an accident? Was he killed by chance because he happened to be in a place where there was an exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was killed on purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I wasn't informed of that case. In any case, I wanted to know about Srebrenica. Do you recall General Mladic, in his letter, expressing his regrets for the killing of a soldier Rensen ^ who wasn't killed by the Serbs. He was actually killed by the Muslims in their attempt to stop him from withdrawing from his location?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this incident was referred to by General Mladic. I don't recall whether -- whether the -- the particulars of what he said. But I do remember it appearing in a letter, the incident appearing in the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall General Mladic and the VRS keeping in mind the safety of UNPROFOR soldiers and that they even sent orders to the units in that regard? There were measures taken to ensure their safety, given the fact that there was a number of reasons which may have caused tension between the members of UNPROFOR and the VRS, due to some attacks on the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall being shown by General Mladic or any of his officers any orders that he issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It wasn't standard practice to send such orders, but I will show you one which was, by way of example. It is 1D644.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is for Mr. Smith to see that, indeed, such orders were issued, and then I can put my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have used the document 1D617, are you tendering it, Mr. Tolimir? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The letter sent by General Mladic to General Smith is something that we wish to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D617 shall be assigned exhibit number D185, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you. And, furthermore, 65 ter document 1D644 does not have English translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since we don't have a translation in English, I will read the heading: "The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, strictly confidential." The date is 12th of March, 1995. Sent to the commands of all corps personally to corps -- to the corps commanders, as well as to the security department which was tasked with providing security to the UNPROFOR. "The mandate of the UNPROFOR in Republika Srpska has been verified by the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska and the most senior levels of government in Republika Srpska. Given that UNPROFOR forces in Republika Srpska are on a peacekeeping mission (irrespective of the fact that both we, the VRS, and its Main Staff and other institutions in Republika Srpska have a number of complaints concerning a biased approach by UNPROFOR members, which is something that is continuing and is being discussed at meetings with UNPROFOR representatives, we are firm in our belief that these UN forces should be accorded full support in the implementation of their tasks. "At the same time as was communicated to the UNPROFOR commanders for the former Yugoslavia and the former B and H, the Main Staff of the VRS, as well as the state leadership of Republika Srpska will keep insisting on full reciprocity and a symmetrical approach to the treatment of the UNPROFOR or the treatment of the UNPROFOR" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: To the treatment of all warring parties by the UNPROFOR equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "We will also insist on the reciprocity the UNPROFOR should display in its relations with Republika Srpska and the VRS." I won't go through the whole document, by General Mladic orders this: "Number 1: Corps commanders will engage all available forces and order searches and other activities needed to be carried out in order to initiate pre-trial proceedings so as to identify the perpetrators of all serious crimes, that they be found and criminal reports submitted, as well as proceedings instituted. The UNPROFOR property needs to be returned," referred to some UNPROFOR soldiers who had their equipment taken en route in Sarajevo to Kiseljak. "Number 2: The security organs and military police units will undertake all measures from their remit in order to identify and sanction the perpetrators of these crimes and that the property be returned to the UNPROFOR. "Number 3: The corps commander -- commanders, will identify the commanders of subordinate units who instigate such criminal activities. They will also do their utmost to establish what happened with the stolen motor vehicles and equipment as well as personal items taken from the members of the UNPROFOR. "Number 4: The corps commanders will submit criminal reports against all subordinate commanders who have been identified as those had instigated the commission of such crimes. "Number 5: Specific measures will be taken against such corps commanders in whose areas of responsibility such criminal acts are -- keep taking place. I will do so personally. "Number 6: The corps commanders will inform me of the measures taken and results achieved at the latest by March 31, 1995." And we see his name below. My question is this: Did you know that General Mladic was personally taking measures against all those committing any type of crime against the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I had not had this letter read to me in this form before. It -- I remember the -- the increase in robberies taking place at check-points, robbery of UNPROFOR equipment and possessions, and this gives -- I complained about it, and this is a -- and then these incidents decreased to a large degree. And here's an example of General Mladic's grip and command of his forces. I -- as I say, I know that this incident or these incidents occurred and that after we'd complained, the situation improved, and now I've seen the letter, or had you read the letter, explaining what -- what General Mladic did at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it's time for our first break. We have to adjourn and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As for this document that is on the screen, could it please be admitted into evidence? Can it actually be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D644 shall be assigned exhibit number D186, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We're going to move onto a different topic, where the commander of the Ukraine battalion was kept as a hostage by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P584, could that please be shown in e-court. It's a situation report for the 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is what it says -- while we're waiting for the report -- oh, here it is. Could we please have page 2 in Serbian. Thank you. Now I'm going to quote what I am interested in. It's the paragraph underneath the diagram, as it were. Can you see here that it's the 17th of July, 1995 and down here it says Bravo and then it says Charlie. I quote: "According to the information received from BritBat through VSAT phone call in the night from the 15th to 16th of July, the Bosnians took as hostage the commander of the Ukraine company, Lieutenant-Colonel Batalin and demanded to give them up all weapons, equipment and ammunition, otherwise threatening to kill the Ukrainian commander. In an hour when negotiations failed" -- And then can we have the next page in Serbian. "16 men from special forces and 100 from regular troops penetrated to Ukrainian company enclose and confiscated all weapons, military equipment, vehicles, ammo and medicine. BiH side supported their actions with fire at the Ukrainian company compound. Only four vehicles left." And then they're enumerated. And then it says: "The BH army threatened displacing Ukrainians as a human shield against BSA attack on their positions." This is my question: Did you receive information, you or your command, that the commander of the Ukrainian company, Batalin, was kept hostage on the 15th and 16th of July as the -- by the BH army in Zepa than all the equipment and weaponry of the Ukrainian company was taken away? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it would be helpful to all the parties to establish what the Defence's position is with respect to this report. Whether it is the Defence's position that this report pertains to the activities of the ABiH in the Zepa enclave, or whether this pertains to the ABiH activities in the Gorazde enclave. I think that is very significant to find out from the Defence what their position is with respect to what this document represents. And I can elaborate further outside the presence of the witness, if the Court feels that appropriate, but I have a firm basis for putting this inquiry to the Defence at this time, to ensure that this document is being properly represented in this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, I note that this document is not listed in the list of documents to be used by the Defence. Secondly, you may deal with that in re-examination, Mr. Thayer. I don't see, at this point, the witness may explain what he knows, in particular, about this incident, which is reported in this report. You, sir, answered the last question of Mr. Tolimir by saying: "Yes, I remember this incident."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can elaborate a bit on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In -- in the -- if you like, in the narrative, the story of the fall of the enclave of Zepa, there is an incident which I think, or thought, this was referring to, when the Bosnian army seize and take the weapons of the Ukrainian detachment. That's what I recall. And I'm -- and reading this particular document, that's what I'm -- was reminded of. And here, I may be out of order, but in the light of the Defence's -- I beg your pardon, the Prosecution's remarks, I have looked at it more carefully and read it in greater detail, and there's a second incident of similar nature in Gorazde towards the end of August. Now without checking, I can't remember all the names of the various Ukrainians involved, but what alerts me to this, now that I have been alerted to it, is the equipment listed as being remaining. And I -- I can't remember there being an excavator in the Zepa pocket, while I think there was one, now I'm thinking about it more clearly, in Gorazde. But other than that I can't be sure. What I recall, and hence my answer, was that there was an incident in which weapons and equipment were seized from the Ukrainian detachment in Zepa. And it's at about this time in the narrative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, again, this is why I precisely stood up now rather than having to spend time on re-examination calling up another document. Clearly the Prosecution has already adduced evidence. There is no question that such incidents occurred in Zepa with respect to threatening the Ukrainian forces there. That is part of our case. There's been evidence, and I think some of that evidence came in through General Smith already. My point is, General Tolimir well knows that General Smith was shown this very document in the Popovic case, and that this document pertains to Gorazde and it should not be the burden on the witness to sort that out when the Defence well knows the provenance of a document and where it is from instead of misleading the witness by suggesting it is from Zepa, when it is not. And when the record in Popovic and the understanding of every party that has used this document before is that that represents an incident in Gorazde. That is my point. It should not be the burden on the witness to undo that. The accused should properly represent the evidence before the Trial Chamber that is he using in his examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What is your position, Mr. Tolimir, to these remarks of Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It is possible that I misspoke, that I said Zepa instead of Gorazde. This is a document from Gorazde, but there was an incident in Zepa as well as the witness had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now this is my question. Because of these incidents that occurred, vis-a-vis UNPROFOR and it was done by the BH army, were Scotland Yard instructions ever followed in hostage situations? Because, as mentioned in the report I just read out, the BH Army was holding an UNPROFOR commander as a hostage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just to be clear on the record, are you now dealing with incidents in Gorazde with this witness? I think it's not part of our case here in this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps Mr. Thayer can say what he has to say, and then I can respond to you. I am asking the witness about his powers as UNPROFOR commander with regard to any kind of excessive behaviour towards UNPROFOR coming from any one of the sides involved. I'm asking whether it was the same. I mentioned by way of a criterion when the Army of Republika Srpska seized the equipment of UNPROFOR, and then I referred to this document too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, in line with some of my prior objections to the examinations, Prosecution has no problem with General Tolimir examining on the conduct of the ABiH in Zepa or, for that matter, in Gorazde. The eastern enclaves, as we've charged in the indictment, comprise Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde is forgotten quite often and it does not figure prominently in this Prosecution, but nevertheless, it sun of the three enclaves that the theory of this case is targeted by the VRS for the squeezing and strangulation. So to that degree we have no objection to questions based on events occurring in Gorazde. I think I understand where General Tolimir is going with the question regarding Scotland Yard but we'll see whether he ties that to a particular time or location, or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I would like to repeat the question of Mr. Tolimir. He asked you: "Because of these incidents that occurred vis-a-vis UNPROFOR, and it was done by the BH army, were Scotland Yard situations ever followed in hostage situations?" That was the question. "Because as mentioned in the report I just read out the BH army was holding an UNPROFOR commander as a hostage."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were no instructions from Scotland Yard that were being followed in any circumstances. I did ask for advice and had some from Scotland Yard on dealing with hostages, but they weren't instructions and they were certainly not a formal advice down through the UN chain of command. This was me seeking advice at the time of the hostage taking in May. The hostage taking by the Bosnian Serbs in May. The -- and the general understanding of that advice formed my -- helped form my opinion of how to behave in -- as a commander in these circumstances thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to clarify my remark about Gorazde. I don't see any reference to Gorazde in the witness summary for this witness. That was my remark, and, therefore, was -- I wanted to clarify if you are now examining the witness in relation to events in Gorazde. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like to add something. In the summary for this witness in the Popovic case, there was no mention of Gorazde. Of course, many aspect of his testimony were not mentioned either. That is not something that the Prosecution is expected to do. However, hardly ever do we see what happened during cross-examination in these summaries and what witnesses said during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. I gave the floor to Mr. Tolimir to continue. And I think your last remark was not in the limits of your role in the courtroom. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, since these are attacks against members of UNPROFOR and about equal treatment of those who take hostages and carry out attacks, I wanted to ask Mr. Smith about these two situations, whether they were treated equally. And were the Muslims threatened, as the Serbs were, all the time. Those are the questions I wish to broach. To see whether UNPROFOR had an equal position towards the sides involved, as regards the use of force and weapons. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So that is my question for General Smith: Whether, in these two cases, when members of UNPROFOR were attacked in Zepa and Gorazde, any kind of sanctions were imposed against the Muslim army. And why is their attitude and enmity towards UNPROFOR not being treated in the same way?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'll deal with the Zepa incident first. I viewed every case of hostage taking equally seriously, and it -- whatever the circumstances. How they were dealt with differed with the circumstances. In the Zepa incident, as I recall it, the situation became increasingly muddled because the Bosnian Serb forces were also holding Ukrainians or it -- in some circumstances, the Ukrainians were disarmed. They were muddled up with the Bosnian Serbs, and it wasn't clear that they had any position of their own at all. And by the time I was in a position to do anything about the Zepa incident, to all extents and purposes, the pocket had fallen, the enclave had collapsed. The fighters were moving into the hills, and we had the refugee problem that we've discussed at some length already. In the case of the Gorazde incident, as I recall it, is that the -- it -- it wasn't long after the incident was reported in the early hours of that following day that I think the British battalion commander in Gorazde got or achieved the release of the Ukrainian officer. But I don't remember that in any great detail, but I think it was the actual hostage situation, was resolved on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, in order to be fair to the witness, I had to call up in e-court P55, paragraph 94, to see that there was this situation in Zepa that the witness referred to as well. We are going to read it out to see exactly what it was. I just wanted to point out these two cases, in order to be able to put my next question. D55, could that be displayed. Paragraph 94. It has to do with the fall of Zepa, the report of Mr. Bezruchenko, who wrote this report as a Prosecution expert and who was in Zepa as well, together with Edward Joseph as assigned by General Smith. Thank you. So can we have paragraph 94 displayed. 9-4, 94 is the paragraph number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we see paragraph 94 in both languages. And you say: "The defenders of Zepa saw the negotiations between their authorities and the VRS as a sign of inevitable collapse of the enclave. In this situation, they no longer cared for cooperation with UNPROFOR and did not need UNPROFOR any longer. In an attempt to seize UNPROFOR's weapons, on the 20th of July, ABiH attacked the compound of the UKR company with heavy machine-gun fire and hand grenades. The second floor was hit with a heavy weapon which destroyed the first aid station and medicine stock. As fighting for the enclave continued, UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo described the situation in Zepa as of the 21st of July, as critical." And that is described by UNPROFOR document -- the UNPROFOR document referred to in footnote 140. Also, it goes to say: "ABiH made threats to kill Ukrainian soldiers which VRS continued shelling of ABiH positions." And then footnote 141, describes that. And then it says: "The ABiH 285th Brigade commander Palic emphasised that a delegation of BHC forward the Ukrainian battalion, UNHCR, ICRC, and UNMOs should get to Zepa by all means. He made repeated threats to kill Ukrainian soldiers if a helicopter with UNPROFOR representatives did not arrive to Zepa." That is document 142, from that footnote. "Meanwhile a UN team on the way to Zepa was belonged in Rogatica by VRS which wanted the ABiH to accept their terms of evacuation of population from Zepa." And then there is this document in footnote 143. "All these developments were taking place against the background of continued VRS shelling of Zepa." Thank you. End of quotation. And now my question: These two attacks against UNPROFOR soldiers in enclaves, did they both happen in July of 1995, on the 20th and 21st? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which two attacks? You've got one in -- that I understand on the -- on the -- going on in -- that's described in paragraph 94. Are you still referring to the one in Gorazde? Because I thought that we'd established that this probably took place in late August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we also see the attack inside Zepa itself during the relevant time. Let us spend some time on that. Were you aware, at the time, that such attack was going on? Were you made aware of that by the Ukrainian battalion in Zepa or Sector Sarajevo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- I knew that this had happened, and the reporting would have come from Sector Sarajevo. I don't think I understood it in -- in the detail that you have in this paragraph, but I knew such attacks were taking place and that threats were being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the BiH Army ever receive air-strikes because of that same thing? How did you solve the situation, generally speaking in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Were their positions ever bombarded because of this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- are we talking about this specific incident? Or are you talking about the whole of the war? What's -- what does the question refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I'm asking you about this particular document. And then, later on, I would like you to tell us whether you ever undertook any sort of offensive action or attack against the Muslims. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, the -- as I recall it, the situation, as it were, resolved itself into another situation, in which the enclave collapsed, the defence collapsed. The Bosnian Serb army occupied Zepa, and the Bosnian army elements retreated into the high ground. And I was able to satisfy myself, or, rather, my subordinates were, that the Ukrainian company, the personnel of the Ukrainian company were safe and were not at immediate risk. I believe on the particular dates at some time on the 21st of July, I'm in London, and I think -- I think that's correct. I think that's the day of the London Conference, so I must have been travelling on the -- at least on the afternoon of the 20th of July, and I suspect the whole of this was actually managed by General Gobillard in my absence, but I can't be sure of that without looking at a diary of my own movements. As to your -- the second leg of your question, there was no occasion in the -- in the time that I was in command of UNPROFOR that air power was used against Bosnian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind that both these documents were drafted before the London Conference - the Gorazde one on the 18th of July, and the Zepa one on the 20th of July - did you apprise the participants of the Geneva Conference of the fact that the UNPROFOR had been attacked by one of the warring sides? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- which Geneva Conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Excuse me, maybe I made a mistake. I meant the London Conference. Did you inform the participants in the London Conference of the fact that the members of the UNPROFOR were being attacked and kept as hostages and that their weapons were taken away from them.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I believe that that was explained to the London Conference by either myself or General Janvier - we were both there at this conference - on -- when it was held on, I think, the 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session because I want to look at some documents that come from the UNPROFOR but they are protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I note again that this document is not listed in your Defence exhibit list. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is on the Prosecution list, and that's why we thought that we could use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Were you personally aware that there had been efforts to prevent you from receiving information about the attack carried out by ABiH on the 20th of July in Zepa on the members of the Ukrainian battalion? So you were prevented to receive this information on the 21st during the London Conference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of what you've just put up on the screen, and I don't -- and I don't think I was prevented from knowing it. I know -- I think I knew this had occurred, as I've told you already. I may not have received a letter about it, but I believe I knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, were the participants in the London Conference apprised of the fact that the BiH army was keeping the UNPROFOR members as hostages? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think they were told that. As I say, by either myself or General Janvier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the reaction of the London Conference to that? Was anything said that something maybe should be done about it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the particular issue being discussed any further. It would have been part of either my report to the -- or General Janvier's, and the matter under discussion in the London Conference was not the specific issue of Zepa and what was going on in Zepa on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So now we saw that the real intentions about the Sarajevo government in relation to Zepa were revealed. Silajdzic wanted the people to stay there; but, at the same time, he wanted the Serbs to have blood on their hands. So can you give a comment about this stance of the Sarajevo government and also give us the basis for your opinion on it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my comment is that I'm not sure that what you've shown me says that. I think that's what Captain Fortin is saying, is his opinion of Silajdzic. I didn't read that and understand it as what Silajdzic has actually explained to Captain Fortin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, when we talk about the UNPROFOR structures and the Sarajevo command and the Bosnia command, did they know at the time that that's what Silajdzic was thinking and that's what he wanted at the time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know what Silajdzic was thinking. And I don't know what -- what -- what we have there is the -- a subordinate officer in the headquarters to General Gobillard's diary, and, as I understand it, that's the opinion of that officer, not the prime minister. And I don't know, you know, on what he bases that opinion when he writes the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you then tell us whether all other officers in the UNPROFOR command also were of the opinion that the Muslims wanted the Serbs to bloody their hands by killing their own people? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't speak for all the officers, or any of the officers in my command as to their opinions. And certainly not at 16 years' distance from the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. We have been discussing the London Conference and the fact that there had been efforts to prevent the participants in the conference to obtain some information. Can you tell us what was the purpose of the London Conference and who participated in it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The London Conference was called by the British government and hence its venue. And from my memory, all the troop-contributing nations to UNPROFOR were invited and, to the best of my knowledge, were present, as were principal -- representatives of the principal NATO allies that weren't already troop-contributing nations. And the purpose of the conference was to -- to announce, to come to and announce a change of direction in relation to the safe areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it was being conducted on the basis of the fall of Srebrenica and the probable and anticipated fall in the light of the circumstances and what was going on of Zepa. And it was also being conducted in the light of the previous -- of the events in May in which air power had been used, hostages had been taken, and the keys, as I've explained to the Court already, were taken away from the military chain of command and from the UN point of view, lodged with the Secretary-General in New York. The result of this conference was that it was decided and announced that any attack on a safe area would be met by the use of air power until it stopped and that this decision was made -- the political element of this decision was made, and the keys were handed back to the military commanders on the ground. That is to say, to the NATO commander in Naples and to the Force Commander in Zagreb, General Janvier. The initial announcement was that this threat of action against a safe area was centred on Gorazde, but shortly after the conference, this was extended to cover all the safe areas that remained.
