And in the following -- the week that followed Srebrenica - I think it was as quick as that but it may have been a couple of weeks - senior officers from the British, France, and America came and explained exactly what the -- this change in the safe area regime was and the threat that was implicit in it to the Bosnian Serbs. I think that's all -- I think that's a summary of the London Conference and its purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, General Smith, I followed your answer to the Prosecution [as interpreted] question, but I wonder whether I didn't miss something. Because it is the second time that the Defence is dealing with this topic. It's the second time that the Defence is alleging efforts being made at the conference to avoid an intervention. This is on line 10 of this page of the transcript. And if we go back to page 45, line 13 of the transcript, we again find a question there, saying that efforts were made, aimed at preventing you to -- from getting certain information about the attacks, the attacks from the ABiH against your troops. So I would -- I wonder whether you could answer this question, because up to now, I haven't got a precise answer to that question. Have there been efforts made aimed at preventing you from getting information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if anyone made an effort to prevent me getting information, but I don't believe I didn't have this information. I knew about this particular attack against the Ukrainians in Zepa. Now, I cannot be absolutely specific at the point I got this information, but I -- I don't believe I was prevented from knowing it, if at all, for very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this answer. But since the Defence comes back repeatedly on that question, I wished to know which -- where the basis for this question. In other words, what kind of efforts could have been made in order to prevent the commander from having information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I find it very difficult to answer this question in that I believe that I was informed. The -- and it was the practice of my command to inform me, particularly of bad news. The -- whether messages were passed very quickly, or delayed for some reason, I just don't know. But at -- I don't have a situation that I can recall when I suddenly found something out that had been concealed from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Judge Mindua. Thank you, General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, in order to illuminate this issue even further, could you tell us the following. Did you ever consider the situation and what was to be done in case of an attack from the enclaves directed at the UNPROFOR, within the protected area? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- the -- the situation of being attacked in an enclave was covered by the need of our detachments to defend themselves, and each detachment was required to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever consider a situation in which you would have to use the authorities given to the commander of UNPROFOR and use the air force, in order to prevent, for instance, taking hostages in the enclaves or taking weapons from UNPROFOR in the enclaves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the situations you're describing, I was not able to use air power. I've told you the keys were taken away from me. Secondly, if it had been a situation of the defence, of self-defence, then I would have had great difficulty in bringing air power to bear because of the close proximity of all parties and the civil population in those sorts of circumstances. Finally, and as I've already explained, the situation of self-defence lasts only so long as the person in question that you're trying to defend is actually being attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, since you say that the -- the authority was taken away from you, can you tell us, did the London Conference give back that authority to you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. It gave -- I had it, as it were, from sometime after the 22nd or 21st of July. At least I had it in theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether the Security Council ever confirmed the decisions made by the London Conference which, after all, is not the Security Council? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall whether the Security Council then confirmed these decisions or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether the Security Council ever gave you the authorisation to use air power against the Bosnian Serb army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insofar as the Security Council resolutions covered the exclusion zones and the safe areas, and insofar that the violation of that safe area was conducted by the Bosnian Serbs, then I think the Security Council had authorised the use of air power.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. You resided in Sarajevo, and that's where UNPROFOR command was. You know that the 12th Division attacked from Sarajevo, which was supposed to have been a protected area. Can you tell the Chamber whether the Muslim army undertook attacks from the protected area of Sarajevo, Tuzla, Srebrenica, and Zepa against the VRS? The list should also include Bihac, because it was another protected area.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian army did attack out of Sarajevo and Srebrenica, as we've said, and in the Bihac, yes. And we can include Zepa as well. I don't think they attacked exactly out of Tuzla itself, but certainly in the vicinity of Tuzla. And they -- and those attacks occurred during 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, can you tell us whether air-strikes ever were ever used to stop Muslim attacks on Serb-held territory when such attacks came from the protected areas of Sarajevo, Tuzla, Gorazde, Zepa, and Bihac?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Air power was not used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to put a question to the witness, a clarification, please. On page 51, lines 6 and 7 you said -- you were asked, did the London Conference give back that authority to you. Then you said: "Yes, it did. I had it, as it were, from sometime after the 22nd or 21st of July. At least I had it in theory." Could you please explain a bit the last part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- first of all, the threat, as it were, hadn't been transmitted to Pale and the Bosnian Serbs, so -- which was part of the decision of the London Conference. So although I would have -- it would have been harder to use if you hadn't actually explained to the other parties what -- what the -- the threat was. So that was one of the reservations. In purely practical terms, the situation as I've explained did -- of this change had not included Zepa, so the fact that we were still engaged in Zepa and all muddled up between the forces and so forth, had not been part of the -- of the decision of the London Conference. This referred to Gorazde and the other safe areas. As I say, that came about a week later, the subsequent decision. So again, in practical terms although I knew this key was now in my pocket, as it were, or, rather, in General Janvier's pocket, it wasn't there to turn yet because these other -- (a), those other safe areas hadn't been threatened; and, (b), we hadn't explained this new situation to the other parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I have another question about the London Conference. Could NATO issue --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Tolimir please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters didn't catch your question. Please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is the given mandate accorded to the UN by NATO or the London Conference? Or was to supposed to have been done by the Security Council of the UN?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I am correct, but the authorities of the London Conference were taken under the United Nations resolutions about the safe areas and -- and the exclusion zones. And, as I've said, I don't know, I can't remember whether or not there was any subsequent resolution by the Security Council. Resolution subsequent to the London Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You bombed Zepa in August, between the 29th and the 30th of August, when there were no civilians or soldiers there, Muslim soldiers. There were only Serb soldiers left. Can you tell us why that decision was made at that time? Why did you bomb Zepa at the time, killing about a dozen Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't recall the -- the particular discussion of that target in the bombing at the end of August, and I would need evidence that we did actually attack a target in Zepa at that time on those days, because I'm not sure we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know when you destroyed what target through air power? For example, Zlovrh was attacked during the night between the 29th and the 30th. An ultimatum was issued that certain targets would be struck unless an RS delegation joined the Serb delegation in Dayton. Could that have been sufficient reason to use air power?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need -- I don't understand what you're -- the basis of this question. The -- I don't recall the UN demanding a RS -- a republican Serb delegation to appear at Dayton against the threat of attacking certain targets. I don't remember that at all. And even if it did occur, it certainly didn't occur on the 29th/30th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. There's also a communique on that issue which we will see tomorrow. There was, indeed, a meeting at which Mr. Milosevic and others arranged it because the Federation did not wish the RS to appear as an independent party at negotiations. They demanded that it be made part of the Serbian delegation, and the HVO had to be made part of the Croatian delegation. My question is this: At the London Conference was any decision made about the evacuation from Zepa? Because, as you say, Zepa was discussed.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall any decision about the evacuation from Zepa. And I didn't say that Zepa was discussed. I said that I or General Janvier, or both of us, would have, and did in my case, report on the situation in Zepa. It's not the same as discussing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I can clarify. At the London Conference, was there any mention of an evacuation of the civilians in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There probably was mention of the evacuation of civilians. The detail of it, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall the general conclusion, was it not to enable the population to go to safer areas where they could receive humanitarian assistance for the duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've just said, there was no conclusion about Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that representatives of the VRS and representatives of the Muslim population in Zepa had begun negotiating as early as the 12th of July, considering the evacuation of civilians and the army from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I knew it as early as the 12th of July, no. I was certainly -- I am aware that there is some form of negotiation going on, and I'm not sure whether this is just before the London Conference or after it, as to when I become aware of this. I think it's -- I think it's probably after the London Conference, but it may not be. I may have learnt it at the meeting when I met with Mladic and, as I recall it, yourself, on the 19th, the day before I travelled to the London Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you learn anything at the time from the Civ affairs representative, Mr. Joseph and Mr. Bezruchenko? Because you had sent them to attend the negotiations on the evacuation of civilians from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I wouldn't have had their reports directly but, no doubt, I was informed of what they were saying. Again, I don't recall on what day it was they were sent in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber what it is that you do remember.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: About what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: About the reports. About the negotiations between the Muslim population and the VRS, which is something you learned in your conversation with General Mladic on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I learnt about it on the 17th. I don't think I met with Mladic on the 17th. I said it was possible I learnt about it from Mladic on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation. I only heard that the witness did not meet with Mladic on the 19th but -- on the 17th, but on the 19th, and then ... the interpretation stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I stopped speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. There's nothing else recorded, and we didn't hear anything else in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. I don't mean any harm. Could we again have D55 which we had on the screen moments ago. It is Viktor Bezruchenko's report. The title of which is: The fall of Zepa. We're interested in page 23, paragraphs 86 and 89. I apologise, 86 and 88. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see it on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, we don't have -- we don't have paragraph 86.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I can see it now in both versions. I wanted to quote from it. "At this point, UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo began preparations for evacuation of civilians from Zepa. UNPROFOR operations order dated 20 July made the following assessment of the situation: BiH defence of Zepa has collapsed and surrender of the enclave to the BSA has been accepted. Large number of DPs wishing to seek refuge in the -- in Federation-controlled territory will therefore have to be moved." There is a document referred to in footnote 131 which is the UNPROFOR order. Next in paragraph 87, it reads: "The order determined the UNPROFOR mission as follows: Together with the BiH government and UNHCR, UNPROFOR is to coordinate the evacuation of DPs from Zepa to Zenica." In paragraph 88, it reads: "The evacuation operation was supposed to be executed in three stagings and involve UNPROFOR forces of Sector Sarajevo, Sector Northeast, Sector Southwest, as well as HQ UNPROFOR (rear)." In support of that, the footnote refers to a document that Mr. Bezruchenko had in mind. My question is this: Since you were a participant to those events, and you responded to some questions put by Judge Nyambe, tell us when the preparations for civilian evacuation began, as regards UNPROFOR? When did UNPROFOR commence its preparations to evacuate the civilians from Zepa? That would be my question.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the -- on the basis of this report that we have on the screen, and I don't know whether it's possible and easy to see the order that is referenced, but my expectation is that what happened and probably being done quite properly by my Chief of Staff as I'm going to London and in the light of the experience of the -- dealing with the refugees from Srebrenica only a few days before, this order was issued by way of preparation so that people were warned as to what they might have to do and who would be involved and so forth. The -- that's what I think this order is likely to be covering and would be, if you like, a prudent preparation for an eventuality of an event that could be anticipated with some certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... If you could clarify, please? I'm not sure if you were recorded correctly: A prudent preparation for an intervention, did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, an event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Event.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't read it as it was coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: A prudent for [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Of an eventuality of an event. Okay. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let us look at another 65 ter document, 02140, which is an OTP document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document has been admitted into evidence yesterday, pursuant to an oral order by the Trial Chamber under exhibit number P2098. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us look at page 3 of the document. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see towards the bottom that it says the document was sent by the Main Staff of the VRS on the 19th of July to the UNPROFOR commander in Sarajevo, General Smith. It reads as follows: "Dear General." It is page 3 in English. We can see it now. It is Mladic's letter sent to you. "Zepa surrendered. The Muslim delegation that I had received at 1800 hours accepted the surrender conditions. "I ask you to inform a representative of the ICRC to be at the check-point in Rogatica tomorrow at 1100 hours. I also ask you to send 50 trucks to transport the population that expressed their wish to travel to the territory of the Muslim-Croatian Federation. Also, four fuel trucks with D-2 fuel and one fuel truck of gasoline should be sent for the needs of the UNPROFOR Ukrainian battalion unit. "I expect you all at the Rogatica check-point at 0900 hours in order to keep an eye on the implementation ever this agreement," et cetera. It concludes with the following words: "I ask you to pass to the Muslim representatives my wish to cooperate in order to conduct this task safely. "Sincerely yours. Commander Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic." My question is this: Do you recall this document; and do you recall any activities undertaken by UNPROFOR in keeping with this letter and in keeping with the arrangement? Did it, indeed, inform the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pretty certain I informed the Muslim side. And I recall the document. I recall this -- the letter from Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Based on that, do you remember that on the 19th, the parties to this conflict, as well as UNPROFOR were familiar with this wish of the population to move out?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I think I'd understood if -- from the meeting with Mladic earlier in the day quite apart from this letter, but I may be running the events together, that the population were keen to be evacuated now that the enclave had collapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If the population wanted to do so, did someone try to prevent them from doing so? Was it done by either the VRS or UNPROFOR or the government in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this stage, do you mean; or do you mean later in the evacuation? I can remember incidents, for example, of people being taken off -- or being reported to me of people being taken off a bus or buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that you recall that, and I will give you an opportunity to address it. But I am now thinking of the situation at the beginning. Did anyone try to prevent the Muslim population from moving out, in keeping with their wishes, be it UNPROFOR, the Serb side, or the Muslim government?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anybody preventing them -- move physically stopping them once someone start to the move. But the negotiations went on for some time. We were still talking about this when I got back from the London Conference, so -- and I'm not entirely clear at this range of the -- of events between the 19th and, let's say, the 24th. But I don't recall a case of anybody being, at that stage, actually being stopped from moving once they were in a vehicle moving. But the -- there was a whole lot of negotiations going on over this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we must have our second break now. And we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We were discussing whether any of the warring sides, or the UNPROFOR, was trying to prevent the Muslim population to evacuate from Zepa. I apologise for repeating the question, but I'm trying to give the context. Your answer can be very short. Simply yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer was no in the specific case. But it is in the context that is where my hesitation lies. It would be the terms under which they left that was the business of the discussion, the negotiation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Sarajevo government want the civilian population in its entirety to leave the Zepa enclave or not? Did you have any discussions to that effect with them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certainly discussions over the movement of the population and where they were to be moved to with the Bosnian government, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us take a look at D60, D60. Let us take a look here at what Alija Izetbegovic said explicitly way back on the 18th of July, 1995. It's a letter that he sent to General Delic. We have it now on the screen but not the English translation. Ah-hah, here it is in English as well, thank you. So I'm going to read the following into the record: "I have just been talking to General Smith. Perhaps I could have women, children and the elderly evacuated from Zepa by UNPROFOR. Would you accept this?" My question is: Was Alija Izetbegovic inclined to accept the evacuation of women, children, and the elderly from Zepa through UNPROFOR, and did he seek the approval from that way back on the 18th of July, 1995, because that's what we can see from this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my meetings with him, I don't recall him being anything but concerned for the civil population in this particular event. I -- I can't vouch for that document. That's him writing to somebody else, General Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, again, I have a problem. This document is not listed in your Defence documents. I don't see who signed this document. Perhaps you can explain something -- I see a date.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, I had to say but didn't that this is the document sent by Alija Izetbegovic to Mr. Delic. It bears his signature. It says Alija Izetbegovic, and then mentions the word Selam. And in item 4, now that I will already explaining it, with he can see that there is a stamp of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Defence received this as part of the disclosure from the Prosecution. So in item 4, to get back to that Alija says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just a moment. We don't see the name, Alija Izetbegovic in this document. Only the first letters, A. I. Just to have it clear on the record. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then maybe we should enter into the record that this was verified by the General Staff communications centre, the cryptographic data protection centre. So the centre certified that it received and transmitted this cable and that it was received from the person who signed it, and whose initials are A. I. And it then went on to Rasim Delic. So in item 4 we found: "An evacuation plan for the population of Zepa has been made here in case that both items 1 and 2 above would fail. I'm sending it to you. "I'm waiting for your answers to the above. "Sarajevo, 18 July 1995. "Selam, A.I.." Which means that it was Alija Izetbegovic writing to Delic. That's the way he signs his documents. We had a witness here who said that this was, indeed, Alija Izetbegovic's signature. However, my question is: Who made this evacuation plan for the population of Zepa? Do you know that? And does this document tell us that this plan was drafted by Alija on his own or in cooperation with the UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who made the plan, and couldn't know unless I saw it, that he is referring to in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any mention of the evacuation of the Zepa population on the meeting that you had with Izetbegovic on the 18th? You told us that you spoke to him on that date.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says I did, and I suppose I did. I don't remember that particular meeting as I sit here. The -- and whether or not -- whether or not we talked about evacuating the population, I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you have problems with interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I heard the last part. I think that was enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I simply wanted to put an emphasis on this, in order for you to realize that this is an authentic document. When he says: I had just finished talk to General Smith. So my question to General Smith was whether he had a conference with Alija Izetbegovic on the 18th of July. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness answered that he doesn't recall on this specific issue and this specific date. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did Alija Izetbegovic, in his meetings with you, ever showed you any short of plan for the evacuation of the Zepa population? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't recall being shown any such plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In items 2 and 3 of this plan, we can see that Alija was considering the possibility of the army going on with the fighting and even to reinforce it with 500 or 1.000 volunteers. Are you aware of any plan by the Bosnian authorities in which they would want to evacuate the population but the army would continue to fight? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D171. It's a document dated 19th of July made by Mehmed Hajric, the president of the War Presidency of Zepa. The document was sent to Alija Izetbegovic on 1300 hours on the 19th. Or, more precisely, 1317; we can see it on the document when it appears on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we move to the next document, Judge Mindua has, in relation to the last document, a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the document was not on the screen but it's back on screen again. Very good. Listening to the answer of the witness, I think I understood that he has not talked with President Alija Izetbegovic about this topic on that specific date and that he has not been aware of any plan concerning the continuation of the fights of the combats on the part of ABiH. So, General Smith, I would like to know whether you had frequent contacts with President Alija Izetbegovic during the first fortnight of July, or let's say during the entire month of July. Have you had any opportunity, any frequent opportunity, of discussing with President Alija Izetbegovic in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say I didn't have this meeting on the 18th, I said I couldn't rather having a meeting, or if I did, what we talked about. The -- as to the frequency of my meetings in -- with Izetbegovic in July, during -- and I don't think I meet with him in the early part of July at all because I'm on leave, if -- and then there is a series of meetings at a greater than normal frequency during the time of Zepa and the London Conference. If -- the number of which I cannot remember and the dates. I'm sure there's a record of these. Each one that I had attended would have been attended by a member of my staff who would have written up a report about it, so if we need to find them, I'm confident that that can be found. And whether they started on the 18th or later than that, I just don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have been checking what has been translated into English but it is exactly what I said. I was wondering whether you had contacts, because in that letter, that seems to be from the president, the president does not talk about a meeting. All he says is that he talked to General Smith. It could have been over the phone. Could it be that you were talking to him over the phone, because then you do not have any assistant that would take down any notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember ever talking to the president on the telephone. These were always face-to-face meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. This will be my last question for the time being. Would it be possible for President Izetbegovic to sometimes talk about his military plans? Let's say battalions that would have to be deployed somewhere, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would not have talked about that to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we should have 1D171 on the screen. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right, now we can see what people in Zepa say. A moment ago we saw that you received something from General Mladic on the 17th. On the 18th Alija Izetbegovic had a meeting with you. He immediately apprised Delic with the fact. And now we can see that on the 19th he notified Zepa about it. We can take a look at the top where it says: "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Army of RBH, Zepa Brigade, strictly confidential." And it goes to Alija Izetbegovic personally, and we can see that it was September by the president of the Zepa War Presidency, Mehmed Hajric. And in the letter he says: "Reply to your memo of 19th of July, 1995 which we received at 1317 hours." So he is replying here. "Dear Mr. President: The telegram is discouraging but we should not lose hope in Allah's grace. I wish to raise several questions. "First what was the Security Council discussing and can the UN compel the Chetniks to allow the entire population to be evacuated, perhaps by helicopter?" So this is what he can ask him on the 19th. "Has a request to ensure such an evacuation been offered to the Security Council?" And item 3: "Do you have any Chetnik prisoners who could be used as a kind of ransom? And then it says please convey our greetings to the Armija and so on and so forth. My question is, can we see from this telegram sent to Alija Izetbegovic as a reply to his earlier letter that the inhabitants of Zepa wanted to evacuate from Zepa and that they wanted to the Security Council to be apprised of that wish of theirs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I go back to the first page, please? I can see that this is a letter. I'm try to see whether it was in reply. It's only [indiscernible] it's a reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You can see in the headline: "Reply to your memo of 19 of July of 1995" [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I beg your pardon. Thank you very much [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... which we received at 1317 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just so we don't have real confusion. Is it the Defence's position that the document that they just showed General Smith is the document to which this reply is replying? I think it's important to find out whether that's their position. Whether there is another document to which the document that is currently on the screen is responding to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would first like to ask the witness, have you ever seen this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Have you any idea if this is a reply to his earlier letter that we have seen on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't -- while I had missed the couple of lines you read to me, I still don't see that it -- that it refers directly, in its responses, to that one that went to Delic. So I don't -- I don't know what he's replying to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This shows us the attitude of the Zepa leadership. Can we now have D54, so that we can see what was Alija Izetbegovic's plan. I asked this witness whether Alija Izetbegovic ever shared his plans with him. The witness was unable to reply, so now I want to show him what it was that Alija Izetbegovic presented as his plan to his associates and the Zepa population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. We now have D54 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is a misstatement. The witness was not unable to reply; the witness said that President Izetbegovic never shared his plans with the witness. This is a big difference. You should rephrase your question. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this is precisely why I stood up before, because General Tolimir well knows that what he has in his hand and could have shown General Smith very easily was precisely what's being called for now. Instead, there's a deliberate attempt to obfuscate what's going on, and only when he is pressed does the relevant document get shown. That is why I intervened before, Mr. President, because he knows that there is this other document that is specifically responsive to the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you heard the concern of the Prosecution. They were asking you not to mislead the witness. I have no idea about the way you are going with this witness, but you should not mislead the witness. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I only want to get a yes or a no from this witness. I never wanted to mislead him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here we can see this document. And it's a letter send by Alija Izetbegovic to the president of the Zepa Presidency, Mehmed Efendi Hajric it was sent on 19th of July, 1995, from Sarajevo, where he says: "Here are my answers to your questions of last night." It means that he is responding to the questions posed by Zepa the previous night. This is his reply to the questions raised by Mr. Hajric. And in item 2, he says: "An evacuation is possible only by land under the supervision of UNPROFOR." Which means that Alija Izetbegovic gives his permission for the evacuation. He goes on to say: "I am in contact with General Smith everyday. The Chetniks are dragging out the talks deliberately. General Smith is guaranteeing the security of women and children. You know that there is no absolute security. As their first condition, the Chetniks have asked that the men lay down their weapons and their investigation and so on, which I refused categorically for reasons I do not need to explain to you." My question is when we look at item 1 and item 2, do we see that Alija Izetbegovic replied to the president of the War Presidency of Zepa when he had asked him whether an evacuation was possible and how it should be performed and under whose auspices? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still not clear whether the document on the screen at the moment is the answer to the document from the war president in Zepa, or it precedes the Zepa document, which is an answer to this one. And I would also make the point that it doesn't give permission for an evacuation. It talks about one being possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I gave you this document so that I could then ask a question. I don't want to ask a question without the document. This is the document sent by Alija Izetbegovic as a response to the previous document sent from Zepa, because he says here at the beginning of this document: "Here are my answers to your questions of last night." And then he says an evacuation is possible. It means he is not against it. He thinks it's possible. He also says that he is in daily contact with you on the matter. He goes on to say that an evacuation should be performed in UNPROFOR's presence and so on and so forth. He also says that an evacuation could only be made by land under the supervision of UNPROFOR. My question is: Did Alija Izetbegovic ask you whether you wanted to perform the evacuation of the civilian evacuation [as interpreted] from Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall being asked such a question. It is quite evident to me, I believe at the time, that should an evacuation be required, then it was my business to make it as safe as possible for those being evacuated. I think that was more an assumption on which everyone was working rather than I was being asked a specific question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you the following. In this document, we see the sentence in item, paragraph 2: "I am in contact with General Smith every day." And you were already asked about the frequency of your contacts to President Izetbegovic. Could you confirm or comment on this sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't know how much he is trying to encourage or impress his subordinate. But it would fit, if the record shows me over those three or four days that I'm there talking to Izetbegovic every day, then that's what was happening. I have no memory as to whether -- not least because in the middle of all this, I disappeared to the London Conference. So I'm not -- you know, this could be every day, every two days and then there's a break of three or four days and I come back again, and I can't recall with any precision at all. But our contacts were frequent during this event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Were there contacts in another way, through other channels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would go to the Presidency and meet him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have a look at the third sentence where he says -- that is the third line in the Serbian. "General Smith is guaranteeing the security of women and children. You know that there is no foolproof security." Based on this, I want to ask you the following. This was stated by Alija Izetbegovic to the president of the War Presidency. Did he ever ask you whether you could provide guarantees, since he seems to be suggesting that you guaranteed the security of women and children, as he wrote on the 19th of July in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't recall the absolute precise words, and I don't think I ever used the word "guarantee." But it's a long time ago, and we'd have to look at the record of those meetings to be sure as to what I had said. There would -- if I had said something as categoric as that, I would be surprised if my staff hadn't written it down in the account of that meeting, whichever one it was that I said it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, General Smith. Could we please look at the third paragraph of this letter of Alija Izetbegovic sent to Zepa. I quote, and I believe you can see paragraph 3 in the English language as well. "My plan: Move out as many civilians as possible, all if possible. The troops stay on and continue to resist. We will do everything to help you by supplying MTS volunteers, and through offensive action in your direction (I believe it is starting today). If we do not succeed in this, you should try to push on on those roads (you know which) but now without the burden of women and children who would in the meantime be taken out." My question is this: Did Alija Izetbegovic have a plan to extract the women and children and did he ask for any UNPROFOR guarantees in order to do so, whereas, at the same time, wanting to continue fighting through the presence of his troops there? Were you familiar with it, or were any of your associates familiar with it during the period when you were absent from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of what is in paragraph 3 was discussed by me -- by me or with me with President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could UNPROFOR have assessed what the plan was of the Muslims in Sarajevo vis-a-vis the population and soldiers in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, we could have and did, no doubt, deduce that such a plan or options were available to them. And, indeed, on the ground, we could see the separation of the men of military age and the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the separation in Zepa carried out by the army or the Muslim civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've -- I don't remember. I don't even know whether I would have known the difference at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, if you know, whether, on the 19th of July, when the letter was received, there was a meeting with the members of the War Presidency at which the Muslim representatives put forth their wish for the entire civilian population to be evacuated from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who was the meeting with?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It is the video recorded meeting that was shown here. Yesterday you saw a excerpt where we see Kulovac, Mladic, Tolimir, and others in attendance.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I just wanted to be sure that's what you were referring to. Of course, I know it was there, I was present at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to make sure we have an accurate record, I don't believe there was any video shown yesterday showing the accused. Perhaps he is thinking about a different meeting on a different day, but the video-clip that was shown yesterday to General Smith did not include the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could check your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question to the witness was whether he knew that at Boksanica on 19th of July there was a meeting with members of the War Presidency of Zepa, at which the Muslim representatives expressed their wish for the entire civilian population of the enclave to be evacuated. And I told him that we saw some footage yesterday showing that on that date there was a meeting, and we see the witness himself on that footage being present in Zepa. I believe some questions were put to that effect by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I -- I think the General is conflating meetings. We well know from the evidence in this case that there were a number of meetings that were held over a period of days in Zepa and at Boksanica, in particular. And the video-clip that was shown yesterday was of a very specific date, and if General Tolimir wants to talk about that specific date, then he can put that date on the record and put that to the witness. If he is talking about another meeting with other participants, then he should put the details of that meeting on the record so it is clear what he is talking about. Because there were a number of meetings, as we all know, with different participants attending different meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you give a precise indication about which meeting you want to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I want to ask the witness the following, and then it is up to him to respond the way he wishes to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will no longer try to jog his memory or offer any suggestions. Did you know that, on the 19th of July, at Boksanica, there were meetings with members of the Zepa War Presidency, and the Muslim representatives at those meetings expressed the wish to evacuate the entire population of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At -- I come back, I was present at a meeting that I know about. Again, without the record of the meeting in front of me, I can't be absolutely sure of the details of the conversation, but the subject of the evacuation of the population was certainly part of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at D55 in e-court. Page 25, paragraph 94 which refers to ... Thank you. We've seen that already; my mistake. My question is this: Did you, in UNPROFOR, given the fact that there were UNPROFOR representatives in Zepa, did you know that the civilian leadership -- that the military leadership as well as the population of Zepa all wished to see the population evacuated to the territory controlled by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew they wished to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. There's an allegation that the Serbs were responsible for the carrying out of that evacuation, but it seems that we all participated in the process of evacuation on the basis of the evacuation agreement.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be quite clear: The situation that the people wished to be evacuated from resulted from the collapse of the defence of the enclave and the presence of the Bosnian Serb army amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether members of the VRS entered Zepa while the civilians were still there? Do you have any knowledge about that; and were you informed of any such thing by your team in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was reported to me that you, amongst others, were in Zepa, that you and the others were armed, and that the -- and were telling the population to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tomorrow we'll see footage about that and how it actually took place. Was I entitled to implement the agreement? This is also something we'll address tomorrow. Perhaps, for the time being, you can offer your view of whether myself or the UNPROFOR representatives present there were authorised to see through the evacuation process, as per the evacuation agreement which was signed by all those involved.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak for anybody but my own command, and they were -- or told by me to be there and to oversee what was happening to the civil population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you referred to yourself and the civilian population, can Bezruchenko or the UNPROFOR commander in Zepa be held responsible for a decision made by the Zepa leadership to evacuate the civilian population for the duration of the war? Could they be held accountable for what happened, if they were merely present there?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're not accountable for the other people's decision, no. But they were accountable for -- to me for reporting and, where possible, maintaining the presence there so as to look after the interests of the civil population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are running out of time. We have to adjourn for the day and to resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom. The court usher will assist you again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 23rd day of March, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
